paras: The burning of Squire Williams's house at Johnston Station was a whitecap attack on the night of January 10, 1903, near Summit, Mississippi, in which a band of "white caps" burned the home of Williams, a Black man, after posted notices had ordered him to leave. The same night the band fired guns on the nearby premises of Sam Caruth, evidently to frighten his Black tenants; no one was reported hurt. First reported in a special to the New Orleans Picayune, the burning ran in wire briefs from Texas to Maryland, and a Jackson dispatch treated it as one of the last acts of a whitecap campaign in southern Mississippi.

Williams lived about two miles west of Johnston Station, near Summit, where the first dispatch was filed. Some weeks before the attack ("some three weeks ago" in the Savannah Morning News) the white caps posted a notice ordering him off his place, with January 1 as the deadline. According to the Picayune's correspondent, Williams had bargained to buy the land and had already made improvements, and after consulting friends and "some prominent citizens" he decided to stay.
A later dispatch from Jackson placed the attack within a series of "whitecap outrages in southern Mississippi," which it discussed alongside the work of "labor agents."

After a second warning a few days before the burning, Williams moved to Johnston Station, and he had nearly finished moving his household goods on the evening of January 10 when his house was set on fire. A separate Summit wire of January 12 said he had left and removed his goods "in compliance with the orders of the marauders" before the raid. From the burning house the band went to Caruth's place in the same neighborhood and fired their guns there, which the Picayune's correspondent read as an attempt "to intimidate his colored tenants."

Sheriff Laggatt (spelled "Leggett" in the Savannah paper) and Deputy Holmes went to the scene and were reported to be trying to apprehend the attackers. No report of an arrest or prosecution for the burning was found in the coverage. The Jackson dispatch of January 20 said that mass meetings of "law-abiding citizens" and "several arrests" had quelled the whitecappers in many communities; it added that the telephone manager at Osyka and Magnolia had refused a whitecap demand to remove telephones from Black homes and offered a $100 reward for those who sent it.

The fullest account was the Picayune's special from Summit, which the Birmingham Age-Herald ran on January 12 under the headline "White Caps Are Giving Trouble" and the deck "Burn an Old Negro's Home." The Savannah Morning News printed a shorter version the same day as "White Caps Busy," and both texts called the attackers "marauders" and "depredators"; only the Age-Herald's fuller text added that Williams "considered it his home." Elsewhere the story shrank to a line in news-brief columns, in the San Antonio Daily Light, the Owingsville Outlook in Kentucky, the Palatka News in Florida and the Grenada Sentinel in Mississippi.

The Baltimore Afro-American, the only Black paper found to carry the story, gave it one sentence on January 17 in its "Latest News in Short Order" digest, saying the house was burned because Williams "did not obey the whitecaps' order to get out." The identical sentence ran the same day in the white Democratic Messenger of Snow Hill, Maryland, so the Afro-American's item came from a shared syndicated digest and carried no comment of its own.

The Jackson dispatch, printed in the Hattiesburg Daily Progress and two days later in the Americus Times-Recorder under "Whitecaps Are Quelled," presented the burning as one of the "occasional echoes" of a movement it called "practically at an end." Baltimore's German-language Deutsche Correspondent headed its version "Weißkappen-Unfug in Mississippi" (whitecap mischief) and described a band that had long terrorized the Black population.

On the second attack, the English-language reports describe the targets as Caruth's "colored tenants" and do not give Caruth's race, while the Deutsche Correspondent called Caruth "another Negro" and said the shots went through his doors and windows. Only the German version said the first notice warned Williams to leave by January 1 if he valued his life.

reader.title: Burning of Squire Williams's house at Johnston Station
bases: A band called 'white caps' posted a notice ordering Williams to leave by Jan. 1, burned his house when the deadline passed, and fired guns to intimidate Black tenants nearby (A1, A3, A10); the burning is one act in a whitecapping campaign, not a stand-alone arson.

The Picayune's Summit special (A1, A3), a separate Summit wire of Jan. 12 (A6), a German-language Summit item of Jan. 13 (A4, A5) and a Jackson dispatch of Jan. 20 (A10) all report the burning of Williams's house by whitecaps after a notice to leave.

accounts.label: Picayune special from Summit
accounts.gist: Williams, ordered off by posted notice with Jan. 1 as the limit, first chose to stay because he was buying the place, then moved after a second warning; the house was burned as he finished moving, and the band then fired on Caruth's premises to intimidate his tenants.

accounts.label: Summit wire, Jan. 12
accounts.gist: Williams had already left and removed his household goods in compliance with the marauders' orders before the house was burned.

accounts.label: German-language Summit item, Jan. 13
accounts.gist: A band that had long terrorized the Black population warned Williams to leave by Jan. 1 if he valued his life; after a sharper second threat he moved, the house was burned, and the band fired warning shots through the doors and windows of 'another Negro', Samuel Caruth.

accounts.label: Black press digest
accounts.gist: Williams's house near Summit was burned because he did not obey the whitecaps' order to get out.

accounts.label: Jackson dispatch
accounts.gist: Whitecaps burned Williams's home near Johnston Station on Saturday night because he disregarded the notice to leave before Jan. 1; whitecap outrages in southern Mississippi were said to be practically at an end.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headed the Picayune special 'White Caps Are Giving Trouble' with the deck 'Burn an Old Negro's Home'; the text called the attackers 'marauders' and 'depredators' and noted Williams 'considered it his home.'
The Savannah Morning News ran the same dispatch as 'White Caps Busy. They Paid a Visit to a Negro, Burning His House.'

The Jackson dispatch treated the burning as one of the 'occasional echoes' of whitecap outrages, said the result sought by both whitecaps and labor agents 'has been brought about', and credited mass meetings and arrests with quelling the movement.
Der Deutsche Correspondent headed its item 'Weißkappen-Unfug' (whitecap mischief) and called the band one that had long terrorized the Black population, a 'wilde Schaar'.
The Baltimore Afro-American printed a single unheaded sentence in a syndicated news digest, the same text as a white Maryland weekly, with no comment.

1903-01-10 is supported; Jan. 12 and Jan. 17 are dispatch/publication dates, and the Jackson dispatch's 'Saturday night' is also Jan. 10
About two miles west of Johnston Station ('Johnson Station' in some papers); Summit is the dateline
Squire Williams (house burned); the unnamed 'colored tenants' of Sam Caruth were the target of the shooting; Caruth himself is a victim only in the German-language version
Supported; add that Williams had bargained to buy the place and that no arrest for this burning was reported

info: Night of Saturday, January 10, 1903 ('last night' in a Jan. 11 dispatch; 'Saturday night' in the Jan. 20 Jackson dispatch)
About two miles west of Johnston Station (also printed 'Johnson Station'), near Summit, Mississippi
Squire Williams, described as 'colored' and 'a negro', whose house was burned; the 'colored tenants' of Sam Caruth, at whose place the band fired guns
None; no crime was alleged against Williams. The burning followed his failure to obey the whitecaps' posted order to leave by January 1.
